pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: `TaggedRecorder` embeds `Recorder`, and both have a `Record` method. Which one runs when you call `tr.Record(...)`, why, and how do you still reach the other one?
expected_points: the outer (shallower) method wins — declaring it on TaggedRecorder shadows the promoted one
promotion is compiler shorthand for delegation through an ordinary field named after its type
the inner method stays reachable explicitly as tr.Recorder.Record — that's how the shadow delegates

questions.prompt: Go has no `extends`. What problems of classical inheritance is it avoiding, and which two Go tools split inheritance's job between them?
expected_points: inheritance problems: fragile base class, premature is-a hierarchies, tight coupling to parent internals, diamond problem
interfaces handle substitutability (behaves-like-a) — embedding alone gives no subtyping

questions.prompt: You have a `Store` interface with three methods and want a wrapper that changes only the writes. How does embedding the interface in a struct save you work, and what runtime trap does it leave open?
expected_points: embedding the interface promotes its whole method set, so the struct satisfies Store while you override only the methods that change
un-overridden calls delegate to the wrapped value with no hand-written pass-through methods
the embedded interface's zero value is nil — the type compiles, but calling a promoted method on a nil field panics at runtime

questions.prompt: You're designing a type that uses another type internally. How do you decide between embedding it and giving it a named field?
expected_points: embedding promotes methods into the outer type's public API — it's a contract decision, not a shortcut
embed when callers should call the inner methods through you (e.g. a wrapper satisfying the same interface)
named field when the inner type is an implementation detail — smaller API, no shadowing/ambiguity surprises, and hand-delegating a method or two is cheap

questions.prompt: `Animal` has `Name()` returning "animal" and `Describe()` returning "I am " + a.Name(). `Dog` embeds `Animal` and defines `Name()` returning "dog". What does `Dog{}.Describe()` print, and why is that the answer?
expected_points: the promoted Describe runs with the embedded Animal as receiver, which cannot see Dog, so its Name call is always Animal.Name
no virtual dispatch is deliberate — the embedded type behaves the same everywhere, which kills the fragile-base-class problem

questions.prompt: A struct embeds two types that both have a `Close()` method. Does it compile? What happens when someone calls `x.Close()`, and how do you fix it?
expected_points: the type declaration itself is legal — same-depth ambiguity only errors at the point of use
calling x.Close() is a compile error because neither method is shallower
fix by naming the field explicitly (x.A.Close()) or declaring Close on the outer type to disambiguate
